explanations.answer: The grace that is in Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: Paul, who wrote this letter, calls Timothy "my child" and tells him to be strong in “…the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” Friend, notice where the strength comes from. It isn't a gym membership. It's grace, and grace is the one thing you never have to earn.

explanations.answer: His own hard training and effort
explanations.explanation: I get why this one tempts you, friend. "Be strong" sounds like a sweaty, grit-your-teeth kind of line. But Paul, who wrote this letter, points Timothy somewhere else: “…the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” Biceps are not in the verse.

explanations.answer: The wisdom of the older leaders
explanations.explanation: Paul, who wrote this letter, doesn't send Timothy to a panel of wise elders here. He says, "You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus." The strength has a name and an address, and it's Christ Jesus.

Paul says the faithful men will be "qualified to teach others as well." Look at that chain, friend. Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, faithful men to still more people. Nobody in that line is supposed to be the end of the line.

Nope, friend, nothing in this verse says to lock it in a vault and whisper about it. The faithful men are to be "qualified to teach others as well." Teaching means it keeps moving. A teaching kept silent can't be handed on.

Scrolls are a fair guess, but this verse never mentions them. Paul says to entrust these things to faithful men "who will be qualified to teach others as well." The job is teaching, passing it on to other people.

Yes, "Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus." Paul doesn't sugarcoat it, friend. He's inviting Timothy to stand right beside him in the hard part. That's the picture of a soldier, and it's honest.

Victory sounds like a soldier word, doesn't it? But Paul's word here is a harder one. He says, "Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus." The invitation is to stand beside him in the hard part.

Training is a good soldier word, friend, and I see why you grabbed it. But that's not what Paul writes. He says, "Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus." He's asking Timothy to share the hard road with him.

explanations.answer: To please the one who enlisted him
explanations.explanation: Paul says a soldier avoids entangling himself in civilian affairs "in order to please the one who enlisted him." The reason is the one he serves. Picture a soldier whose eyes stay on his commander. He's not looking over at the sale on the other side of the street.

explanations.answer: To earn a higher rank someday
explanations.explanation: Promotion is a sensible guess, friend, but Paul never mentions rank. The verse gives the reason: "in order to please the one who enlisted him." His eyes are on the one who signed him up.

explanations.answer: To keep himself out of danger
explanations.explanation: Staying safe sounds logical, but think about the verse right before this one. Paul has just said, "Join me in suffering, like a good soldier." So safety isn't the point. The verse says the soldier does it "in order to please the one who enlisted him."

Paul says a competitor "does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules." Think of a runner who cuts across the middle of the field and shouts, "I finished first!" Great speed, no crown. The rules decide it.

Schedules matter, friend, I live and die by mine. But Paul's word here is a different one. A competitor doesn't receive the crown "unless he competes according to the rules." Showing up on time won't win it if the rules get skipped.

A plan is a nice thing to have, but Paul's word is "rules." The verse says a competitor doesn't get the crown "unless he competes according to the rules." You can have the best plan in the stadium, friend, and it still has to follow the rules.

Careful, friend, Paul flips this one around. He says, "The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops." First, not last. I think of it like the one who baked the batch getting the first cookie off the rack. That's just fair.
That's right, friend. Paul says, "The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops." First in line, not last. The farmer did the work, so he gets the first taste.

Paul says, "Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things." The insight comes from the Lord. Timothy is asked to think about the soldier, the athlete and the farmer, and the Lord is the one who gives understanding.
Elders are a sensible guess, friend, but they don't appear in this verse. Paul says, "…the Lord will give you insight into all things." The insight comes from the Lord.

The church is a good thing to lean on, friend, but Paul names someone else here. He says, "Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things." It's the Lord who gives the insight.
That's right, friend. Paul writes, "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David." Raised from the dead is right there in the verse. It's the center of the gospel Paul proclaims.
This one is true, friend. Paul says, "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel." Raised from the dead is part of what Timothy is told to remember.

Paul says, "But the word of God cannot be chained!" He's in chains himself, and he still says that with an exclamation point. Paul can be chained like a criminal, but the word of God stays free. I'd put that on a banner.

His spirit is a nice thought, friend, but it isn't what Paul says. He's chained like a criminal, and then he says, "But the word of God cannot be chained!" The word of God is the thing that stays free.
The verse doesn't mention the church in Rome, friend. It does say Paul is chained like a criminal for the gospel. Then he says, "But the word of God cannot be chained!" That's what stays free.

Yes, Paul endures all things "so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory." The elect are the ones he's enduring for. He endures all of it for their salvation.
With chains in the picture, freedom sounds close, friend. But Paul's word is a different one. He endures "so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory."

Rest sounds lovely after all that enduring, doesn't it, friend? But that's not the word Paul uses. He endures all things "so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory."

explanations.answer: If we deny Him He will also deny us
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "if we deny Him, He will also deny us." That's the warning in the saying, friend. It's a serious line, and Paul puts it right in the middle of the promises. Every line in this saying is worth taking seriously.

explanations.answer: If we rest He will take our crown
explanations.explanation: That line isn't in Paul's saying, friend. The saying has pairs like "if we endure, we will also reign with Him," and one warning: "if we deny Him, He will also deny us." Nothing in it takes a crown from someone who rests.

explanations.answer: If we doubt Him He will walk away
explanations.explanation: That one sounds close to the last line, but the last line goes the other direction. Paul says, “…if we are faithless, He remains faithful…” The warning is this one: "if we deny Him, He will also deny us."
Paul says, “…if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.” The reason is who Christ Jesus is. His faithfulness doesn't depend on ours. Friend, that's a rock to stand on.

That's a kind thought, friend, but it isn't the reason Paul gives. He says, “…if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.” The reason is who Christ Jesus is. It isn't how hard we tried.

Paul doesn't give that as the reason, friend. The verse says, “…if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.” The reason is who Christ Jesus is, and Paul puts it right there in the line.
